brief: A ZeroHedge compilation stitches together three takes on long-end Treasury stress. Goldman's Rich Privorotsky says the long end is still totally bidless: PCE came in lighter and an October hike looks less likely, but the market has only priced hikes out of the front end, the back end still doesn't care, and the rapid rise in yields has triggered historical red flags that need to calm. BNP Paribas's Florian Roger puts 5.5% on the 10-year as the level where equity-market pressure kicks in, and yields are nearly there. Bloomberg's Simon White argues Treasuries look cheap against stocks, GDP, bunds and a 60bp fair-value gap, yet buyers haven't emerged; being this statistically cheap historically does not mean oversold, so prices could fall further before a durable bounce, and his leading indicator points to real yields still rising. He flags reflexivity risk (higher volatility worsening Treasury liquidity) and fiscal strain (one of the world's largest deficits and interest bills) as reasons yields could keep climbing, and above 5.25-5.50% Treasuries start correlating positively with stocks, eroding their hedge value. Shorting is risky given government-intervention prospects (Treasury hired Jefferies' David Zervos to manage debt maturity), but that is not a reason to buy either.
